overview: This bill, the Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2025, sets funding targets and policy for the U.S. Coast Guard, the branch of the armed forces that handles maritime safety, search and rescue, drug and migrant interdiction, and port security. It authorizes spending for fiscal years 2025 through 2029, including about $11.3 billion for operations in 2025 rising to $15.5 billion in 2029, and raises the authorized number of active-duty members from 44,500 to 50,000 and eventually 60,000. It creates a new civilian Secretary of the Coast Guard, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, who would report directly to the head of the department the Coast Guard sits in. Other parts cover buying ships and aircraft (including limits on using foreign shipyards), merchant mariner licensing, vessel and port safety, drones and uncrewed vessels, oil spill response, and a long list of changes to how the Coast Guard prevents and responds to sexual assault and harassment, especially at the Coast Guard Academy. The House passed it, and as of July 23, 2025, it had been sent to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
for: Supporters say the Coast Guard has been stretched thin and underfunded for years, and this bill gives it more people, newer equipment, stronger civilian oversight and overdue reforms to protect members from sexual misconduct.
against: Critics say the steep growth in authorized spending and personnel may not be matched by actual funding, and adding a new Secretary with its own staff could add bureaucracy to an already strained service.
